newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sharif scents win in Pakistan polls, foes cry foul.
newsitem.headline: Sharif scents win in Pakistan polls, foes cry foul.

text.p: Former prime minister Nawaz Sharif said his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party was heading for a big victory in Monday's elections and asked his rival, ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, to accept defeat.
"The results are coming in indicating that the PML is winning the elections," he told reporters in his home city of Lahore.
The Election Commission had announced his party's victory in only two parliamentary constituencies after midnight.
Earlier, he told cheering crowds outside his home in Lahore, capital of the populous central province of Punjab: "We are winning from all over the country."
Leaders of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) and of the Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement (MQM) complained of vote-rigging and irregularities.
But the leader of a Commonwealth team of observers said the elections had been free and mainly peaceful.
"As the polls closed, it was a picture of largely peaceful elections, a relaxed election day," former Australian prime minister Sir Malcolm Fraser told a news conference.
"We are satisfied that those who wished to vote were able to vote, and in the way they wanted to, without any sense of oppression and without any sense of coercion," he said.
Many of Pakistan's 56.5 million eligible voters stayed away from the polls, either because of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan or because they distrust current political leaders.
Sharif said he was "very satisfied" with unofficial results received so far for the 217-seat National Assembly. "It looks like we will certainly cross a decent majority," he said.
President Farooq Leghari called national and provincial assembly elections -- being held on the same day for the first time -- after dismissing Bhutto on November 5.
He accused her government of corruption, nepotism and extra-judicial killings in Karachi and the Supreme Court ruled last week that the president's action had been justified.
Senator Iqbal Haider, a senior PPP spokesman, met the Chief Election Commissioner to complain of widespread rigging and irregularities, the official APP news agency said.

First results had been expected by 10 p.m. (1700 GMT), but the first official result, giving the only National Assembly seat from Islamabad to PML, was announced well after midnight, eight hours 45 minutes after the voting had closed.
Later, the PML won another seat in the nearby Rawalpindi district.
Commentators on the state television said the PML also took an early lead in the provincial assembly elections in Punjab and the North West Frontier provinces.
"We are heading for a landslide in Punjab (and)...in the Frontier," Sharif told reporters after midnight.
He said his party would get a sizeable number of National Assembly seats in Bhutto's home province of Sindh and two or three seats from 11 in the southwestern province of Baluchistan.
"But we are not going to declare victory until we are sure of the results probably tomorrow morning," he said.
Eight people were killed in election day violence.
Five were shot dead when two groups at odds over a land dispute clashed near a polling station in Gujranwala in Punjab, police said.
Two more men were killed in Punjab's Gujrat and Vehari districts and one at Khanpur in the North West Frontier province.

In the southern city of Karachi, two MQM supporters were killed and three wounded, an MQM spokesman said, blaming a rival MQM faction for the attacks and accusing army troops of standing by while MQM supporters were intimidated.

About 250,000 troops were deployed for the elections, which were monitored by observers from the United States, European Union, Commonwealth and South Asia, as well as the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan. Several polling stations opened late.

"The country needs a strong and stable government," said Sharif, who served as prime minister from 1990 to 1993, when he was sacked by the president, restored by the Supreme Court and then persuaded to resign before losing a general election.
He promised not to seek revenge on Bhutto for alleged victimisation of his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) while she was in power and said he would not put her on trial.
He said the opposition and government should have a working relationship. "So what she did to us, we will not do to her."
Qazi Hussain Ahmad, leader of the religious Jamaat-i-Islami, which boycotted the polls, said voter apathy had vindicated his party's rejection of the "corrupt electoral process".
He said he hoped the people would now "stand by Jamaat-i-Islami in bringing about a grand Islamic revolution".
Bhutto voted in her home village in Sindh province. "People are voting for the arrow because they want stability, they want democracy," she said, referring to the PPP's election symbol.
Cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan failed to cast what would have been his first vote in an election.
"Unfortunately the Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) could not field a candidate in my constituency so therefore I am abstaining," he told reporters in Mianwali, his home town.
Imran is standing in nine other constituencies for his Tehrik-i-Insaaf, as permitted under Pakistan's electoral law.
Leghari pledged a swift transfer of power to a new government and denied charges by Bhutto, a former ally and now a bitter foe, that he planned to rig voting in 65 constituencies.
"There will no delay in the transfer of power even by a single day," Leghari said. "There should be no confusion."
